column2: Rauschenberg glues the sheets of paper into a long strip and lays it out on the pavement of Fulton Street; he coats a section of the roadway with ink; Cage, at the wheel of his Model A Ford, drives through the ink and then straight along the paper, taking care only not to run off it; the tire track prints along the whole length. Words: Rauschenberg in an interview: Cage was there because he was the only one with a car; he only had to stay on the paper, and he did an excellent job Atmosphere: A New York street, black ink, the engine of a Model A Ford, a public and slapstick experiment Stakes: Making organized chance and the direct trace the material of art

The exhibition is coldly received, with no sales and scant, icy criticism; only one visitor counts: John Cage, the avant-garde composer Words: Stuart Preston (New York Times): “stylish doodles in black and white” Atmosphere: public failure, the seed of a decisive friendship Stakes: failure as encounter

Cage stands before Rauschenberg's white canvases and feels a competitive imperative: he must write his silent piece, or else music is lagging behind painting. Words: “Oh yes, I must—otherwise I'm lagging, otherwise music's lagging” Atmosphere: A thrill of friendly emulation beneath the Zen calm Stakes: The alleged birth of 4'33"

Olson and the cook's young nephew come upon a local auction; the child exclaims “It's like a race”; struck by the echo of slave auctions, Olson writes an immediate poem, dedicates it to Alvin and the Shahns, and gives it to Ben Shahn. Words: “It's like a race” Atmosphere: Sudden, uncomfortable, revealing Stakes: The word race, between a contest and a racial category, in the segregated South

The two young men, standing on the patio, look at a large canvas covered with tar; they throw handfuls of pebbles at it; Motherwell, between them, gestures and says “More”; they throw again; “More”; they throw again; “More”. Words: Motherwell: “More.”, repeated three times Atmosphere: A teaching ritual under the older painter's eyes; gesture rather than discourse Stakes: The passing on of the creative gesture: accident, material, and action count as doctrine

Doubting his strength, Goodman enters a decade of purgatory (“a useless time”); he challenges himself to find an ounce more strength and finishes the fourth volume of The Empire City with no hope of a publisher; in the novel, his hero loses heart, goes temporarily mad with conformity, then recovers and ends up “spoiling for a fight”, looking for a fight he does not know. Words: the hero does not know which fight, nor how to get into it; Goodman knew that his own duel would be with the organized System made flesh, outside fiction Atmosphere: dark, then combative; clear-sightedness about powerlessness Stakes: the passage from novelistic abstraction to real social confrontation

One spring evening, the author sees a woman in black coming toward her, a lace shawl over red hair, walking fast, eyes lit by her destination, crossing the street without seeing her; the author, new to the scene, stares at her; her friend identifies her. Words: The friend: “That must be Elaine de Kooning”. Atmosphere: Energy, haste, joyful eagerness; the city as adventure (probably a party, to dance, drink, and laugh). Stakes: The mythmaking of Elaine: even unknown, she radiates.

A reporter for the Yale student newspaper finds that most students are producing nonobjective abstractions, a dramatic change from the Surrealist paintings of two or three years earlier, attributed to Albers's reorganization of the courses.

Olson leaves for Yucatán with his wife Constance, hoping to decipher the Maya hieroglyphs; he writes Creeley visionary letters that become Mayan Letters. The title “Mayan Letters” is a pun on the Maya glyphs Consequences: The letters are his fullest statement of his project

Seventeen letters to Robert Creeley, dated February 18 to July 1, 1951, mixing lyrical anecdotes (the wounded seabird), reports from snake-infested fields, anthropological speculation, and literary strategy. 17 letters; Creeley is called only “lad”; the letter of March 17 begins with “christamiexcited”; the “f” key of his typewriter breaks and sets off a string of curses ending in “fuck it” Consequences: Publication by Divers Press, Majorca, 1953

From the window of a third-class bus on the coast road, Olson makes a discovery (“christamiexcited”); he and Constance come back with bags of sherds, little heads, and feet; the next day, alone, farther south, he digs up his first hieroglyphic stone. Bags of sherds & little heads & feet; third-class bus; letter of March 20, 1951

From the window of a third-class bus, Olson spots something; he and Constance come back with bags of sherds and little heads and feet; the next day, alone, pushing farther south, he digs up his first hieroglyphic stone; breaking off a letter to Creeley, he writes that his nerves are strained too hard toward the ruins. Words: “christamiexcited”; “I am wild for it”; “Christ, these hieroglyphs… Is, in fact, verse. Is their verse.” Atmosphere: Fever, excitement, the dust of the digs Stakes: The poet turns archaeologist to prove that an imaginative leap can succeed where the academy fails

In the spring of 1951, the last members of the conservative group withdraw; Duberman argues that the college then becomes, for the first time, a resolutely American and resolutely radical environment. Consequences: Transition to the college's American radical era

In the morning, after breakfast, Connie shows the visitors the campus: the rusty snakebite kits along the road, the library, the Studies Building with its individual studies, the sunny terrace, the painting studio, and the studios. Snakebite kits never opened, rust stains; there are rattlers and copperheads, but they mind their own business; mist lifting from the peaks; growing humid heat; ~100 studies for a capacity of 99 students; a three-level concrete building. Consequences: Rumaker begins to feel at home at the college.

A large, cool white room with a gray floor and no finished painting: canvases of various sizes used as palettes, smeared with oil paint, turpentine, and linseed oil. Connie points to a small canvas in a corner as a painting she likes; Rumaker takes it for a brush rag. Phyllis Franklin comes in through the back doors and stares at her canvas with an intensity that astonishes Rumaker. Canvases smeared with color, dribblings, smudges; a mountain stream rushing past the windows on the shady side; the Eye and the Stables, two long white buildings serving as painters' studios. Consequences: Rumaker's first lesson at Black Mountain: before what he does not understand, keep quiet and open his eyes; a decision to come back at all costs.

A walk to Roadside lodge under the pines: Roger and Rumaker on the second floor, Marge and Mary Ann on the third (separation of the sexes for form's sake, ironic since Mary Ann is the only one in the group who is not gay). Introduction to students under the pines, including Mark Hedden, an anthropology student from Westport, Connecticut, who will later play a large part in Rumaker's life. Rooms of unpainted pine, sour-smelling mattresses, an old chest of drawers, straight-backed cane chairs; a smell of damp and mildew; a carpet of dry pine needles; a wooden footbridge over a deep ravine; Streamside cottage, a faculty residence; the college farm beyond the creek; Mary Fitton Fiore will later say that the area has the highest rainfall in the region and that the Seven Sisters deprive many rooms of sun.

On Saturday, Marge drives the group to Asheville to visit Thomas Wolfe's boardinghouse, the setting of Look Homeward, Angel, kept as it was since his mother's death, then Riverside Cemetery, where Wolfe has been buried since 1938. Rumaker and Mary Ann, devourers of Wolfe, are in a secret fervor; Roger snickers; Marge is bored. A wide porch, high-backed rocking chairs, the room where Ben died of pneumonia, Wolfe's father's spidery handwriting around the old telephone; inscription: “Tom, son of W. O. and Julia E. Wolfe… A Beloved American Author… 'The last voyage, the longest, the best…'”; the Pack Library, where Wolfe as a child read everything; Marge in a short-sleeved sport shirt. Consequences: Strengthens Rumaker's vocation as a writer.

First appearance of Charles Olson, whom Rumaker has been waiting for since Ben Shahn's lecture in Philadelphia. Saturday night roast chicken (a tradition), prepared by the cooks Malrey and Cornelia with the help of students. Olson and Harrison dominate the conversation with knowing banter; Olson makes Rumaker and Mary Ann feel that they are very special people. A dozen tables in a row on the long porch; a dress-up evening: Lou Harrison in a dazzling vanilla-ice-cream suit with a thick dark brown goatee; Connie in a plain blue blouse, denim skirt, loose-knit shawl, thin-strapped Greek sandals; Olson: nearly seven feet tall (2.10 m), a long brown seersucker jacket, a faded blue work shirt, a misshapen tie, chino work pants, high-topped work boots, horn-rimmed glasses. Consequences: Rumaker is won over; Olson awakens in him the desire to be there and to be near him.

After dinner, Olson takes Mary Ann and Rumaker in his old blue Ford convertible, probably to fetch something at the drugstore for their daughter Kate (born eight months earlier) and perhaps an ice cream at a drive-in he likes. Olson drives fast, one big hand on the wheel, talking over his shoulder; Rumaker, silent, is spellbound by the full moon over the valley. The driver's leather seat pushed far back from the wheel by Olson's weight; top down; wind in their ears; a moon enormous and closer than ever seen; 12 miles to Asheville. Consequences: Rumaker's surrender to the college is complete.

On Saturday afternoon, ill at ease or deciding the place is not for them, Marge and Roger leave in Marge's Chevy to see the local sights and do not come back until Sunday, the planned day of departure. Consequences: They leave the college after the weekend; Roger goes back to Rider for his degree.

She had long since concluded that she could not be both a serious artist and a mother; her son Jeff is raised by his grandparents, and she sees him only on emotionally charged weekends (as told in a recent New York Times best seller). Weekends only; money to buy materials Consequences: An illustration of what Alice Neel called a terrible dichotomy

Everyone is back from spring vacation, and classes resume that morning; Dawson has been moving rocks, which has taken off some fat and built up his back. A book he had ordered arrived the same day. Rock-moving chore, strengthened back

A walk along the road lined with rusty lampposts and tall vegetation; Rumaker is uneasy at the snakebite kits but dares not ask anything; Connie, guessing, assures them that no one has ever been bitten. Words: There are rattlers and copperheads, but they mind their own business. Atmosphere: Lifting mist, the first burning sun, unease soon calmed by Connie's composure Stakes: A first trust in the place

Connie points to a small canvas in a corner as a work with dynamic and interesting forms; the group stares politely, murmuring; Phyllis comes in, answers “oh,” then absorbs her canvas with her eyes; Rumaker looks at it a second time and glimpses a muscular energy beneath the chaos. Words: Connie: doesn't he find that she has achieved dynamic and interesting forms? Phyllis: “oh.” Atmosphere: Coolness, the roar of the stream, polite unease mixed with dazzlement Stakes: Rumaker's aesthetic conversion; a decision to come back

First appearance of Olson, a giant in brown seersucker, who falls upon the platter of chicken while being all courtesy; in-jokes between Olson and Harrison that make the neighboring tables laugh; Rumaker and Mary Ann dare answer only in monosyllables; Olson makes them feel they matter. Words: In-jokes not understood; Olson's and Harrison's laughter dominating the room Atmosphere: Human warmth, excitement, a reassuring strangeness; laughter that shakes the rafters Stakes: Rumaker falls under the spell; hope of a queer enclave

After dinner, off to Asheville (errands for baby Kate, perhaps an ice cream); Olson drives with one hand, talking over his shoulder; Rumaker, hypnotized, watches the full moon flood the valley. Words: Olson's words carried off by the wind, inaudible to Rumaker Atmosphere: Wind, top down, moonlight of a quality never seen before Stakes: Rumaker's complete surrender to the place

Crossing Pack Square, a visit to the untouched boardinghouse (Ben's room, the father's writing around the telephone), then the cemetery, where Mary Ann and Rumaker reverently read the stone; Roger jokes, Marge is bored. Atmosphere: Youthful romanticism, a secret fervor hidden from Roger Stakes: Confirmation of Rumaker's vocation as a writer
Cage writes to Boulez that he has read a great deal of Artaud, thanks to him and to Tudor, who was reading Artaud because of Boulez. English translations were rare.
One of their blueprints is shown in the exhibition “Abstraction in Photography,” under the title “Blueprint: Photogram for Mural Decoration.” MoMA, May-July 1951 (German version: May-June)
One of their blueprints is shown in the exhibition “Abstraction in Photography,” under the title Blueprint: Photogram for Mural Decoration. Catalog title: Blueprint: Photogram for Mural Decoration
First edition, set, laid out, printed, and bound by the author himself at the college print shop, in a cream paper cover. 12mo, cream cover

Williams visits Miller a month before entering Black Mountain: Miller is avuncular, funny, enthusiastic, encouraging; Williams sometimes beats him at Ping-Pong. Ping-Pong (like beating Proteus) Consequences: Miller will later (probably) introduce Harry Partch to Williams

Before joining Black Mountain, Williams goes to San Francisco to see Rexroth, Duncan, and Henry Miller, and produces his first Jargon Press book there: a small broadside of one of his poems with an engraving by David Ruff. Broadside, engraving by David Ruff Consequences: The birth of Jargon Press (Jargon #1)

The college publishes a magazine made up entirely of work by students and teachers. Contents: a Noh play by Nick Cernovich, “High Speed Computing Machines” by Natasha Goldowski, poems by Russell Edson and Joel Oppenheimer, “Father” by Fielding Dawson. Only one issue appears; a second is typeset, but there is no money to print it. Editorial work shared among Richards, Oppenheimer, Fitton, Kemeny, and Larsen. Consequences: Shares its name with the 1954 magazine, whose editors Olson and Creeley apparently did not know of it.

Back from his months in Yucatán, Olson presents a version of his essay “Human Universe” as a lecture before fifty members of the 1951 summer session; the essay appears the following winter in the fourth issue of Origin, then in 1954 in Robert Creeley's edition of the Mayan Letters. Fifty listeners Consequences: Publication in Origin No. 4 (winter 1951-52), then in the Mayan Letters (1954)

During the 1951 summer session, fired by Olson's enthusiasm for glyphs, Katherine Litz dances The Glyph to a score of the same name by Lou Harrison; Ben Shahn paints A Glyph for Charles (thick letter-like strokes projected onto a human torso like musculature); the multimedia “Glyph Exchange” brings together Olson, Litz, Harrison, and Shahn, who designs sets and a motif for the dance of the student Nicholas Cernovich. The photograph of Litz dancing The Glyph is taken by Teri Helen Dick
Besides The Glyph, Harrison and Litz collaborate in the summer of 1951 on Chorales for Spring; the composition Adjustable Chorale was flexible enough to allow the choreography to develop.
Lou Harrison is recommended to Black Mountain by John Cage for the 1951 summer session. Consequences: Harrison at BMC, summer 1951
Gablik attends Black Mountain College in the summer of 1951, where she gets to know Rauschenberg. Consequences: The beginning of a friendship of nearly two decades.

The 1951 summer session with Ben Shahn and Robert Motherwell; Olson knew Shahn from their days at the Office of War Information in Washington. Consequences: Dawson calls that summer strange and difficult, like the year before.

Back from Yucatán, Olson reads “Human Universe” before fifty members of the summer session: the West from Socrates to the camps, experience interrupted, the shared flesh of the Maya on the buses. Words: action “absolutely interfered with”; touch as “the natural law of flesh” Atmosphere: Prophetic urgency, a small but captive audience Stakes: The college itself as a polis dying and being reborn

During the 1951 summer session, Gablik, a young student, gets to know Rauschenberg, back at the college for the summer. Stakes: the start of a twenty-year New York friendship spanning the world of the avant-garde

A month after visiting Henry Miller at Big Sur in June 1951, Williams goes to Black Mountain College. Visit to Miller in June 1951, departure for BMC in July Consequences: The beginning of Williams's tie to the college and to Olson

Callahan teaches in July and August alongside Siskind, invited by Hazel Larsen Archer; he finds the music and dance especially stimulating and judges the college freer and more democratic than the ID, despite a disorganized administration. A remembered remark: they paid them almost nothing and hardly fed them, since the students had eaten all the food during the winter. Consequences: Callahan and Siskind's first extended work together; Siskind accepts the post at the ID for the fall.

Invited by Olson, whom he had known at the Office of War Information in the 1940s, Shahn arrives at the end of July 1951 to teach painting and give lectures; he stays four weeks and takes full part in the life of the college, collaborating with the dancers. A four-week stay; the other visual arts teacher that summer is Robert Motherwell; the same year sees the publication of his biography Portrait of the Artist as an American Consequences: An invitation to represent the United States at the 1954 Venice Biennale; a palimpsest turn in his painting

Olson, with Alvin, nephew of the college's African American cook Jack Lipsey, attends an auction where a Black boy says “Like a race”; Olson draws from it a poem meditating on the word “race” as word, image, and event. A silver coin passed from hand to hand; “the whites' eyes”; “the seats / theatre soft”; “feel / the weight” Consequences: The poem “Glyph (For Alvin, & the Shahns)”
Olson completes two dance plays that summer, Apollonius of Tyanna and The Born Dancer, evidence of his interest in integrating music, dance, and poetry.

Olson stands next to Alvin in the doorway; the boy's foot crosses the threshold and his voice draws the white people's eyes; the New Yorkers pass a silver coin along the rows to feel its weight; the Southerners, idle on a summer evening, bid dollar by dollar; Alvin says “Like a race” and Olson is not sure he heard. Words: “Like a race, the Negro boy said / And I wasn't sure I heard, what / Race, he said it clear” Atmosphere: an overlit room, soft seats, palpable racial tension, the weight of money Stakes: the word “race” as an abstraction applied to a living body; the material of the poem Glyph

Harrison arrives at the shore of Lake Eden four years after a breakdown that took him to the psychiatric ward of Presbyterian Hospital in New York; his distress is still acute. Consequences: Two months later he finishes the vocal score of Rapunzel.

Cunningham proposes that Asawa and Lanier work on her house on Greene Street (where she has lived since 1947), repainting two rooms, a bathroom and a hallway, in exchange for three years of photographic coverage of their two toddlers; she buys all the paint and photographic supplies. Proposed contract: two rooms (bathroom and hallway) for three years of photographic coverage; paint and supplies paid for by Cunningham. Consequences: Cunningham will go on photographing the Asawa-Lanier children well beyond the three years, in several dozen pictures.
In the fall of 1951, Olson offers a course titled Hieroglyphic Writing and Ovid's Metamorphoses.

In September 1951, Laverne inquires about someone who could design his new showroom in San Francisco; he also inquires about Asawa's textile designs. Consequences: Later collaboration with Lanier and Asawa

A poem printed as a folded 2-page broadside, written to be read in Olson's absence at the Moby-Dick centennial celebrated by the Melville Society at Williams College, Labor Day weekend, September 2-4, 1951; slipped into a paper folder; a special edition with an abstract drawing hand-colored by Charles Oscar. Folded broadside, 2 pages, weekend of September 2-4, 1951

Dan introduces Fielding to Franz on the second evening; the warmth of the handshake and of their eyes establishes an immediate reciprocity between two strangers. Fielding had earlier avoided Franz in order to watch him from a distance. A warm handshake, a look Consequences: The beginning of a very close friendship that lasted until Franz's death

At the Cedar, Franz calls Black Mountain “downtown Manhattan,” including the college in his own experience; Fielding laughs with pride. Consequences: Fielding feels proud to belong to Franz's experience

Franz asks Charley his age: forty-one. Franz, condescending and smug, says he is older. Charley, hurt, stares at him as if to say this was not what he expected. Steps, the tree, the bench, the millstone Consequences: Franz's rejection of Charley, the price of including Black Mountain in Franz's world
After Charley praises Roosevelt's charm, Fielding retorts that that is what killed him. Charley, surprised: “By God, that's right!”

Fielding had written a beautiful one-page story, had it framed, and gave it to Franz for Christmas; years later he comes across it by chance among old junk at the back of Franz's closet. One page, a frame, Christmas, the back of a closet Consequences: A lasting wound

A slim, pink-and-white, red-haired girl arrives six weeks late in the fall of 1951. M.C. introduces her to Fielding, who shows her around; she is tense, defensive, smokes filter cigarettes with a Ronson lighter. A freshly starched shirt in small red and white checks, button-down collar, three buttons open, white pants, white sneakers, copper hair brushed back, a Ronson lighter Consequences: She will change the lives of two women students; Fielding will fall in love with her and sleep with her
She says she is a writer, working on a novel about a girl she knew; the girl is dead. They walk in silence; then she says it is too soon and she will tell him about it someday.

M.C. has tea while reading Ulysses before her class; she questions Fielding about the new girl in a “lady lawyer” voice and guesses at his confusion; Fielding thinks the new girl is “gay”; then she goes off to make “espresso.” Class with Alex and Cicely (perhaps Pat and Russell). The college's only clock, on the Dining Hall stove; coffee in a mug; rolling a cigarette; espresso

Dinner together, choosing a study, moving in; beer brought by someone, records; Tim knocks with three cans of beer; Victor cries “Behold! ... a lady!” as he stumbles; they read poems to one another, steal wine, drink the dregs of the home brew, peanut butter sandwiches in the Dining Hall.

She recommends Djuna Barnes's Nightwood as her favorite book; wears a heavy ID bracelet that she slides up and down her forearm; the only Williams she has read is Tennessee; Fielding quotes Charley, Pound, Frobenius to her. Heavy ID bracelet

A chubby girl, a fan of Eddie Fisher and Ted Williams, becomes a hardened, armed Miami cop, run into in a gay bar in the Village; the other, shy and hollow-cheeked, becomes icy and bitter, sneering at the mention of Black Mountain. A dark gay bar, a farewell karate chop, “first class bastard” about Ted Williams

Sitting cross-legged in the hallway at night; Fielding sterilizes a razor blade in the flame of a match and cuts each thumb; they suck, join their bleeding thumbs in the air, and swear “I, Fee, will never forget”; they kiss, then part to go to class. Razor blade, match, a cut in the thumb, blood Consequences: The five then scatter (Kitty, Hitler, and Dancer gone; Farmboy comes back, then leaves for good)
At twenty-one, Fielding opens a story with “Monday is a metaphor” (the alliteration amuses him); at Black Mountain, naming a metaphor was a natural act; a metaphor was as plain as a potato.

Speedy, a middle-aged student (not fast at all), writes a poem about the lake and spells “mirror” as “mirrow”; the misspelling is accepted and becomes fact; Charley yells “LOOK AT THAT GODDAMNED WORD!” A misspelling turned into a word

Fielding checks: the valley's horned beetle is a stag beetle, but a different one (older, humpbacked, with a longer and wider body), proving, according to Charley, that the valley was primeval. Hump, elongated and widened body
Years later, Franz introduces Fielding to Ornette Coleman in exactly the same warm way Dan had introduced Franz to him; Fielding is struck and filled with admiration.

Adamic dies at fifty-two of a gunshot at his farm in New Jersey; his death is officially ruled a suicide. Rice, who knew him too well, remains convinced it was a violent crime: no note, no clear motive, the farm set on fire at about the time of his death while Stella was away. Adamic had been investigated by HUAC in 1948 for left-wing associations. Stella out of town; the farm on fire; NYT of September 5, 1951 Consequences: Rice, devastated, loses his closest friend.

Franz asks Charley's age, learns that he is forty-one, and answers condescendingly that he is older; Charley stares at him, hurt, as if to say this was not what he wanted Words: Franz: “I'm older than you are.”; Charley's look: “But Franz, this isn't what I — this isn't IT!” Atmosphere: sudden tension, a mute wound under the trees Stakes: the failed meeting between the great poet and the painter, two men with similar values

Standing at the bar in the light from the window, the glass of beer becomes a flash of crystal; Franz drinks, sets the glass down, murmurs, sucks the foam, turns around, winks, and speaks; around them, Louie in a white apron, the bottles, the taps Words: “Boy! The first one's always the best.” Atmosphere: crystalline light, sensuous fullness, revelation Stakes: Franz as initiator: the world of things speaks through him

A guided tour; a pause on the rising curve; she contemplates the lake and the valley and flicks her cigarette into the tall grass with an impatient gesture; a dialogue about how long (“Two years” / “It'll be longer”); a visit to the Studies Building and the farm, back to the lodges; a conversation about her novel and the dead girl Words: “Gee, it's beautiful.” / “Been here long?” / “I love it.” / “She's dead.” / “It's too soon. I'll tell you about it again. Some time.” Atmosphere: tension, the newcomer's wariness, a hand trembling as she smokes, a final smile Stakes: an erotic and literary encounter; a mystery (the dead girl) planted for later

Fielding gets a coffee, sits down across from M.C., who is reading Ulysses, tips back his chair, and rolls a cigarette; M.C., in a low, grave voice, guesses that he wants to talk, plays the lawyer, and asks the question he is waiting for; he admits he finds the new girl “gay” and interesting; she turns the question around, and he defends himself; she makes an espresso and leaves for class Words: “Well, Fielding. It's clear you want to talk.” / “What do you think of the new girl?” / “Don't you think it's because she's so new?” Atmosphere: complicity, grave humor, tea and espresso, the secret trembling of Fielding's hand Stakes: M.C. reads Fielding's heart; he discovers he is in love

After dinner together, the newcomer settles into her study; shared beers, records; Tim knocks, three cans in hand, scratching his head; Victor stumbles backward: “a lady!”; they read poems to each other and tell stories; the beer runs out; stolen wine, the dregs of the home brew, sandwiches in the Dining Hall, then bed Words: Tim: “I've brought three cans of beer.”; Victor: “Behold! ... a lady!” Atmosphere: smoke, an open window, ragged gaiety, a depressing end with no beer Stakes: the integration of the newcomer; the small bohemian ceremonies of the dying college

Sitting cross-legged in front of the study; Fielding sterilizes the blade with a match, cuts his thumb, sucks it; each does the same; thumbs joined in the air, bloody, an oath with their names; hugs, then parting: there is class Words: “I, Fee, will never forget.” Atmosphere: a solemn and childish ritual, night, the urgency of classes Stakes: warding off the inevitable scattering of the community

Speedy reads or writes his poem about the lake with “mirrow” for “mirror”; the whole community, and Charley above all, is seized; the misspelling is adopted as a fact Words: “LOOK AT THAT! LOOK AT THAT GODDAMNED WORD!” Atmosphere: collective wonder, a burst of sacred laughter Stakes: error becomes poetry: the essence of Olson's teaching

The streetlamp is often out; Fielding stops in the dark, barefoot, hands outstretched, sensing the possible snakes; he yields to the darkness, takes in the night, listens to the slow rock under his feet and the damp on his half-naked skin Atmosphere: a dense darkness behind vision, a frightening and wonderful stillness, the threshold of the universe at his fingertips Stakes: the mystical union of the body and the primeval valley

Adamic, 52, is found shot dead while Stella is out of town; the farm catches fire at about the time of his death; no note, an uncertain motive; the official verdict of suicide is disputed by Rice and many friends. Atmosphere: Mystery, violence, fire. Stakes: The loss of Rice's dearest friend; a plot suspected after the HUAC investigation.

Aware of the financial difficulties, Robertson and Carl Kent ask Doyle (the farmer) and Wes Huss whether there is an alternative enterprise to the farm; Doyle suggests cutting the pines on a plot that can be cleared; the Board provides the capital, they buy two double-bit axes and sell the pulpwood to a local mill; after two weeks they get a chainsaw that multiplies their output Two double-bit axes, a chainsaw bought after two weeks, pines cut for a pulp mill Consequences: Output and sales rise but are not enough against the growing deficit; the two students leave for New York, sensing that the end of the college is near
The birth of the Hardings' son, when the temperature on the mountain often drops below freezing by mid-October Temperature often below 0°C (32°F) on the mountain

Fall and winter 1951-1952: the faculty sets aside time to discuss its educational aims, an echo of the 1930s; the official minutes preserve the lively exchanges between Olson and the two new social science appointees. Consequences: Gradual clarification of Olson's project

Excavation, the culmination of Bill's abstract-Surrealist style, appears in the Sixtieth Annual American Exhibition and receives the Logan Medal and the purchase prize. Logan Medal, purchase prize Consequences: Institutional recognition begins.

Two months after his arrival, Harrison finishes the vocal score of a fifty-five-minute opera, a nearly verbatim setting of William Morris's poem (1858) after the Grimm tale “Rapunzel.” A twelve-tone opera, three voices, two characters, six short acts. Consequences: Act III will win a prize in Rome in 1954.

Rauschenberg writes to the dealer Betty Parsons to promote his White Paintings, in language described as Edenic, on Black Mountain College letterhead, the year he meets John Cage at the college. College letterhead; phrases such as “presented with the innocence of a virgin” and “Today is their creater” (sic, for creator) Consequences: The text suggests that this language of whiteness anticipated the rhetoric of the blank page of Cage/“Meyer” at the beginning of the following decade
Dawson writes Mother in October 1951, unpublished until this book; with At The Farm, the only one of his stories devoted to the daily life of the college. Consequences: Read in Olson's class.

Reading Mother aloud, Olson stumbles over the HO HO HEY DROP passage and stammers with embarrassment; Dawson, embarrassed, says he has the rhythms wrong; Mary suggests letting Fee (Dawson) read. The story passes from hand to hand until it reaches Dawson, who reads it as it is written; afterward each person reads his or her own text, then Olson reads his new poems and lays out the teaching formula he is building. Order of passing: Olson to Nick, Joel, Mary, Duck, Victor, Cynthia, then Dawson. Consequences: A change in teaching: each student reads his or her own work and the discussion follows; Olson and the students learn together to listen.

Aware of the deficit, the two students propose an enterprise to the farmer Doyle and to Wes Huss; at his suggestion they fell and limb pines with axes for two weeks, sell the pulpwood, get a chainsaw from the Board that multiplies their output, then give up for lack of sufficient results Atmosphere: extremely hard and slow work, the exhilaration of the venture, the sadness of leaving Stakes: saving the bankrupt college, a failure

Olson reads the students' work aloud; reaching the HO HO HEY DROP passage of Mother, he breaks off, tries, and gets so flustered that he stammers; Dawson, embarrassed, tells him he has the rhythms wrong; Olson tries again and fails; Mary suggests letting Fee read; the story passes from hand to hand to Dawson, who reads it as it is written; from then on everyone reads his or her own text, discussion follows, then Olson reads his new poems and builds his teaching formula under the group's questions. Words: Dawson: the rhythms are wrong. Mary: why not let Fee read? Atmosphere: Embarrassment, stammering, then release when Dawson takes over the reading; mutual attention, Olson on the alert. Stakes: The reversal of the master-student relationship: Olson stops being the only reader, and the class becomes a listening community.

A series of meetings (October 25 and November 2, 9, 21, 28, and 30, 1951) debating the reform of studies; on November 2, Olson declares that he believes in the absolute freedom of the student, even the freedom to concentrate on a single subject. Minutes preserved at the Raleigh Archives Consequences: Prepares the reorganization into institutes

During a record cold spell with snow and ice, Elaine slips on the ice and breaks her right leg while visiting the Empire State Building. Convalescing in Denby's apartment (he had left for Italy), she is sketched by Kaldis in her cast, skirt pulled up to show how high the cast goes on her thigh, right foot on a pillow, another pillow clutched in her arms, with a how-did-I-get-into-this-mess expression; Kaldis emphasizes her fingernails and toenails as if to suggest bright red polish. Cast reaching high up the thigh; nails outlined in pencil; a record cold spell with snow and ice Consequences: Weeks in a wheelchair, then crutches; she hires a lawyer (who writes speeches for Adlai Stevenson's campaign); the first vote of her life, for Stevenson

Elaine breaks her tibia and fibula in early November 1951; in an undated letter to Josef Albers, she says she is done with the wheelchair, crutches, and canes. Albers's reply, dated April 18, 1952, celebrates her recovery. “wheelchair, crutches, canes, etc.”; letters preserved at the Josef and Anni Albers Foundation Consequences: Evidence of a lasting correspondence between Elaine and Albers after BMC
Olson document dedicated to Cy Twombly, November 1951.

Convalescing, her skirt pulled up to show the height of the cast, her foot on a pillow and another pillow clutched to her, she poses; Kaldis emphasizes her nails as if painted red Atmosphere: the self-mockery of an invalid in the thick of social life Stakes: a fall (literally) at the height of the art scene

Meetings devoted to educational ends: Adams asks why there are so few academic courses and argues for a disciplinary pattern in the first two years, denouncing aberrant students and the risk of chaos; Olson answers that the right term is historical, that BM works toward living knowledge and not the history of knowledge, that there has never been any other pattern than the passionate interest of the person teaching; two weeks later Sprague tries to pin Olson down on his special educational pitch, and Adams ends up doubting that anyone understands Olson; Olson retorts that there is something to be gained by not planning a curriculum. Words: Adams: many students are aberrant personalities, too wrapped up in themselves; there is a considerable lack of historical knowledge. Olson: this place goes blind, and it is as legitimate to go blind in education as anywhere else. Olson: the individual is more complex than any curriculum. Adams: he doubts that anyone here knows what Olson is talking about. Atmosphere: Good-natured but substantive sparring, Olson's torrential style against methodical questioning Stakes: Two conceptions of education clash: the survival of the “new” Black Mountain depends on it
Correspondence with Erwine Laverne (New York showroom): Lanier speaks of Ruth's “wire stuff”; an undated draft letter by Ruth, around 1952. Term: “wire stuff”

In the throes of a romantic crisis, Rivers slashes his wrists one afternoon; he recovers at Fairfield Porter's, who paints him with symmetrical bandages and a dazed look; Elaine, in her letter, dismisses his fear of a nervous breakdown as a lack of vitamin B, judging him so lively and exhibitionistic Symmetrical bandages; a fanciful diagnosis: vitamin B deficiency

Still convalescing in the spring of 1952, Elaine accepts Porter's invitation: she went for two days and stayed two weeks, doing nothing but painting, eating, talking, reading, and sleeping; with Porter busy writing his articles, she takes a mischievous pleasure in working in his studio and helping herself to big tubes of his paint that she cannot usually afford. Big tubes of paint borrowed

Driving with Mercedes Matter and her family: she finds the subjects of the large Renoirs vulgarly beautiful, jokes about Barnes's humor in making Picasso a reliable but mediocre second-stringer, and remarks that the large Seurat and Cézanne's Large Bathers seem to her like enlarged reproductions, so familiar is a painting one has never seen. Renoirs vulgarly beautiful; Picasso a second-stringer Consequences: An anticipation (translated only in 1968) of Benjamin's problem of mechanical reproduction
